stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of the NAACP legal strategy: Houston and Marshall; Sweatt v. Painter and McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents (1950); Brown (1954); Brown II (1955).
stimulus.text: Paraphrase of the NAACP's legal strategy as described in the books. Beginning in the 1930s, NAACP lawyers led by Charles Hamilton Houston and then Thurgood Marshall attacked segregation in graduate and professional schools first. In Sweatt v. Painter and McLaurin v. Oklahoma State Regents, both decided in 1950, the Supreme Court ruled that separate graduate schools were not equal. In 1948 the NAACP decided to attack segregation itself, rather than asking only for equal facilities. The cases were combined as Brown v. Board of Education, decided in 1954. A second ruling in 1955, Brown II, told schools to desegregate 'with all deliberate speed' but set no date.

stem: Sweatt and McLaurin together showed that 'separate but equal' was failing because of which of the following?

options.text: The Court ordered all public schools desegregated in 1950 at once

The states refused to defend segregation in court at all

rationales.A: Background from the books: the Court did not order all schools desegregated until Brown in 1954.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Texas built a separate law school and Oklahoma admitted McLaurin only under restrictions, and the Court found both unequal.
rationales.C: Background from the books: Texas and Oklahoma defended segregation in both cases.
rationales.D: Background from the books: both cases reached the United States Supreme Court, which decided them in 1950.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: in Sweatt, Texas built a separate law school for Black students rather than admit Sweatt.
2. Background from the books: in McLaurin, Oklahoma admitted McLaurin but made him sit apart in class, the library, and the cafeteria.
3. Background from the books: the Court ruled both arrangements unequal, in Sweatt for the school's standing and in McLaurin for the restrictions on learning.
4. Separate facilities failed the test even when states tried to provide them.
Remember: a doctrine fails when its own test keeps coming back unequal.
